The nesting ground of the Kirtland's warbler was first discovered in 1903, and at that time its breeding range was very little larger than it is But this bird is rather particular about where it will build a nest, using only dense stands of pine trees not over 12 feet tall. Such habitat is contrary to efficient silviculture and jack pine, which was the kind of tree that most frequently grew in the stands the warblers preferred, was most common in unmanaged timber stands following fire. So progress in timber management and fire control was the threat to the Kirtland's warbler. Probably less than 300 pairs of warblers survive today in half a dozen Michigan counties. Prospects for this warbler are reasonably bright, however, once suitable sites have been acquired by State and Federal agencies and a rotation plan for maintenance of suitable nesting habitat has been completed. As if the Kirtland's warbler doesn't have enough problems, cowbirds, which never make their own nests, hatch their own eggs, or rear their own young, persist in parasitizing Kirtland's warbler nests. The result is that the young cowbirds survive at the expense of the young warblers. Cooperating agencies have begun a reduction of cowbirds during warbler nesting periods. The rate of parasitism has been noteably reduced. The resulting impact will affect little more than the small area where the species now nests in Michigan.
The Utah prairie dog, true to its name, is, and always has been, found only in southwest Utah. Campaigns from time to time have sought to eliminate this competitor for grass. Today, only about 6,000 of this species remain, confined to parts of three counties. While the Utah prairie dog is not atypical to the grassland biome it occupies, it is hemmed in by other close relatives of the same Genus Cyonmys, and is therefore effectively isolated. Successful restoration of the animal to its former range would impact probably no more than eight or nine counties in Utah.
